subject: math
domain: Statistics and Probability — Making Inferences and Justifying Conclusions
cluster: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies

items.prompt: A researcher randomly assigns $80$ patients to take either a new blood-pressure drug or a placebo for $8$ weeks, then compares the two groups. Classify this study as a sample survey, an experiment, or an observational study.

steps: Check whether the researcher imposes a treatment. Here the researcher decides who gets the drug and who gets the placebo, so a treatment is being imposed.
Because the researcher actively imposes a treatment and compares the resulting groups, the study is an experiment.

items.prompt: A pollster phones $1{,}000$ registered voters chosen at random and asks whether they approve of the mayor. Classify this study as a sample survey, an experiment, or an observational study.

steps: No treatment is imposed on the voters; they are only asked a question, not given something to do.
Because a representative sample is measured to estimate a characteristic of the whole population of voters, the study is a sample survey.

items.prompt: Over one year, a clinic records the daily step count and resting heart rate of $300$ adults without telling any of them to change their behavior. Classify this study as a sample survey, an experiment, or an observational study.

steps: The clinic only records measurements and does not impose any treatment or tell anyone to change behavior.
Because subjects are observed and measured without intervention, the study is an observational study.

items.prompt: A city wants to estimate the proportion of all residents who recycle at home. State the purpose of conducting a sample survey for this question.
items.answer: To estimate a population parameter, namely the true proportion of all residents who recycle, by measuring a representative sample instead of the entire population.

steps: A sample survey measures a representative sample rather than the whole population.
Its purpose is to estimate a population parameter. Here that parameter is the true proportion of all residents who recycle at home.

items.prompt: Define the difference between random sampling and random assignment in one sentence each.
items.answer: Random sampling means selecting the subjects for a study at random from the population; random assignment means allocating the already-chosen subjects to treatment and control groups at random.

steps: Random sampling happens when subjects are chosen: it picks who is in the study at random from the population.
Random assignment happens after subjects are chosen: it splits them into treatment and control groups at random.
In short, sampling selects subjects from a population, while assignment allocates subjects to groups.

items.prompt: A study selects $400$ adults at random from a national health registry, then randomly places each adult into an exercise program or a control group. Identify each use of randomization and state what each one accomplishes.
items.answer: Selecting the $400$ adults from the registry is random sampling, which makes the results generalize to the population. Splitting them into the exercise and control groups is random assignment, which makes the treatment comparison valid for a causal conclusion.

steps: First randomization: choosing $400$ adults at random from the registry is random sampling. It reduces selection bias so the results generalize to the population in the registry.

Second randomization: dividing those adults into program and control groups at random is random assignment. It balances confounding variables across the groups so the comparison supports a causal conclusion.
So this study uses random sampling for generalizability and random assignment for causation.

items.prompt: Researchers observe that students who eat breakfast tend to score higher on tests, but they never assigned anyone to eat or skip breakfast. Can they conclude that eating breakfast causes higher test scores? Explain.
items.answer: No. This is an observational study, so it shows only an association; a lurking variable could cause both, so causation is not justified.

steps: No treatment was imposed; the researchers only observed who ate breakfast, so this is an observational study.
An observational study can reveal an association but cannot establish causation because confounding variables are not controlled.
For example, a stable home routine could lead both to eating breakfast and to higher scores, so the breakfast-to-scores link may not be causal.

items.prompt: A school district wants to know whether a new reading curriculum raises reading scores. Recommend an appropriate study design and justify your choice in one sentence.
items.answer: Use a randomized comparative experiment: randomly assign students to the new curriculum or the current one, because only random assignment supports the causal claim that the curriculum raises scores.

steps: The question asks whether the curriculum causes higher scores, which is a cause-and-effect question.
Only a randomized comparative experiment can justify a causal claim, so randomly assign students to the new curriculum or a control curriculum and compare their scores.
Random assignment balances confounding variables across the groups so any score difference can be attributed to the curriculum.

items.prompt: Explain how random assignment lets an experiment support a cause-and-effect conclusion.
items.answer: Random assignment balances confounding variables across the treatment and control groups on average, so any difference in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment rather than to a pre-existing difference between the groups.

steps: Confounding variables are traits (such as age, diet, or motivation) that could affect the outcome and differ between groups.
Random assignment spreads these traits evenly across the treatment and control groups on average, so the groups start out comparable.
Because the groups differ only by the treatment, any difference in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment, which justifies a cause-and-effect conclusion.

items.prompt: A pollster randomly selects $600$ residents and asks which of two parks they prefer. A classmate calls this an experiment because it uses randomness. Identify the study type correctly and explain why it is not an experiment.
items.answer: It is a sample survey, not an experiment, because no treatment is imposed on the residents; the randomness is used only to select a representative sample.

steps: An experiment is defined by imposing a treatment on subjects, not merely by using randomness.
Here the residents are only asked a question; nothing is done to them, so no treatment is imposed.
The randomness selects a representative sample, which makes this a sample survey rather than an experiment.

items.prompt: An observational study finds that neighborhoods with more ice-cream sales also have more swimming-pool accidents, and a reporter concludes that ice cream causes pool accidents. Name a plausible lurking variable and explain the mechanism by which it produces the association.
items.answer: Hot weather is a lurking variable: warmer days raise both ice-cream sales and the number of people swimming, which increases pool accidents, so the two rise together without ice cream causing the accidents.

steps: The reporter draws a causal claim from an observational study, which can only show association.
A lurking variable is one that influences both measured quantities. Hot weather fits: on hot days people buy more ice cream and also swim more.
More swimmers means more chances for pool accidents, so hot weather drives both variables up at once.
Therefore the association is explained by the weather, not by ice cream causing accidents.

items.prompt: A researcher randomly assigns volunteers who responded to an online ad to one of two diets and finds the first diet lowers weight more. To whom can the causal conclusion legitimately generalize, and why?
items.answer: The causal conclusion applies to the volunteers studied because random assignment justifies causation, but it may not generalize beyond people like these self-selected volunteers, since they were not a random sample of any larger population.

steps: Random assignment was used, so a causal conclusion about the diet is justified for the subjects in the study.
However, the subjects were self-selected from an online ad, not randomly sampled from a population.
Without random sampling, the results may not generalize beyond people similar to these volunteers, so the scope of the conclusion is limited to that kind of person.

items.prompt: A study claims that taking a vitamin causes fewer colds, based on observing that people who choose to take the vitamin report fewer colds. Critique this conclusion and state a corrected, defensible conclusion along with the design that would justify a causal claim.
items.answer: The causal claim is not justified because the data come from an observational study where people chose whether to take the vitamin, so a confounding variable such as overall healthy habits could explain the difference. A defensible conclusion is that vitamin use is associated with fewer colds. To justify causation, run a randomized comparative experiment that randomly assigns subjects to take the vitamin or a placebo.

steps: Subjects chose whether to take the vitamin, and no treatment was imposed, so this is an observational study that can show only association.
A confounding variable such as generally healthier habits could cause both vitamin use and fewer colds, so the causal claim is flawed.
The defensible conclusion is that taking the vitamin is associated with fewer colds, not that it causes fewer colds.
To support causation, use a randomized comparative experiment: randomly assign subjects to a vitamin group or a placebo group so random assignment controls confounding variables.

items.prompt: An experiment randomly assigns patients within a single hospital to a new therapy or standard care and finds the new therapy works better, but the patients were not randomly sampled from any larger group. State which type of randomization is present, which is missing, and what each fact costs or supports for the conclusion.
items.answer: Random assignment is present, which supports a causal conclusion that the therapy works better for these patients. Random sampling is missing, which costs generalizability, so the causal result may not extend beyond patients like those at this hospital.

steps: Patients were randomly assigned to therapy or standard care, so random assignment is present. This balances confounding variables and supports a causal conclusion for the patients studied.
Patients were not randomly sampled from a larger population, so random sampling is missing.
Random sampling is what provides generalizability, so its absence means the causal result cannot be safely extended beyond patients similar to those at this hospital.
In summary, the design justifies causation for these patients but not generalization to a broader population.

items.prompt: A town reports that years with more lifeguards on duty also have more drownings, and an official proposes removing lifeguards to reduce drownings. Identify the lurking variable, explain why it reverses the apparent relationship, state what study design could establish the true causal effect of lifeguards, and explain what randomization that design relies on.
items.answer: The number of beachgoers is the lurking variable: busier years bring both more lifeguards and more swimmers, and more swimmers means more drownings, so lifeguards do not cause drownings. The reported relationship is an association driven by crowd size, not a causal effect. To establish the true causal effect, run a randomized comparative experiment that randomly assigns comparable beaches or time periods to have lifeguards or not, relying on random assignment to balance confounding variables across the groups.

steps: The data come from observing towns over years, so this is an observational study that shows only association.
The lurking variable is the number of beachgoers: crowded years lead the town to staff more lifeguards and also put more swimmers in the water.

More swimmers means more drownings, so crowd size drives both lifeguards and drownings up together. Removing lifeguards would not lower drownings, so the proposed action is based on a confounded association.
To find the true causal effect, use a randomized comparative experiment that randomly assigns comparable beaches or periods to have lifeguards or not.
That design relies on random assignment, which balances confounding variables such as crowd size across the groups so any difference in drownings can be attributed to the lifeguards.
